title: May The Rain
description: A solitary journey across a rain-washed, surreal mountaintop, told in fifteen minutes with pixel art, silence, and illustrated interludes.
releaseStatus: Released · Windows download; untested Linux build offered
imageAlt: Original AI-generated dreamy painterly editorial illustration of a traveler on a rainy tepui, looking across misty waterfalls toward a warmly lit pavilion; not game imagery
imageCredit: AI-generated editorial concept art — not official game artwork or gameplay
article: Some games ask for eighty hours. May The Rain asks for ten or fifteen minutes—and places its entire journey on a lonely mountain. Its creator, Ziyanthus, describes a surreal, foggy tepui where the rain has washed away every soul. The premise is spare enough to fit on a postcard: a lone presence reaches a place where no life seems to belong. The unanswered question is what brought that presence there. Rather than advertising a huge world to conquer, the game presents a small landscape to look at carefully.

The developer calls it a two-dimensional, walking-simulator-adjacent narrative. You move with the arrow keys or WASD and interact with Z or the space bar. It also includes several illustrated cutscenes presented in a visual-novel-like fashion. That combination interests me because it gives a tiny project two distinct storytelling instruments: the player's movement through a landscape and the deliberate framing of an illustration. One leaves room to wander; the other can hold your attention on a chosen image.

Pixel art is sometimes associated with speed, nostalgia, and crowded screens. Here, the advertised ingredients are the opposite: fog, emptiness, a mountain, and rain. A low-resolution image does not have to be busy to be evocative. In a game organized around an absence of life, the things that are *not* drawn may matter as much as the objects that are. That is a reason to be curious about May The Rain, not a claim about how it feels to play; this feature is based on the creator's description rather than a completed playthrough.

The production story is as interesting as its premise. Ziyanthus says the art, writing, programming, design, and music were all created solo in one month. It was the creator's first Godot project, made with Godot 4.5 for an October 2025 game jam. That is quite a lot of disciplines compressed into a very small window of time. The downloadable release is listed for Windows, with an untested Linux build included. The creator flags depictions of gore and self-harm, as well as implicit sexual imagery, so this is not necessarily a gentle or family-friendly excursion.

If you enjoy compact, atmospheric experiments that don't demand a long-term commitment, this looks like an intriguing stop. It is exactly the kind of work this archive ought to preserve: a small, personal creation that could easily be missed while everyone is looking at next year's blockbuster.

title: ElecHead
description: A little robot conducts electricity through everything it touches—and throws its own head to solve puzzles in a darkened factory.
releaseStatus: Released · October 14, 2021 (PC); also available on consoles
imageAlt: Original AI-generated dreamy painterly editorial illustration of a small brass robot throwing its lantern-like head amid glowing machinery and vines in an abandoned factory; not official gameplay
imageCredit: AI-generated editorial concept art — not official game artwork or gameplay
article: Most puzzle-platformers treat electricity as something to avoid. ElecHead makes it something you carry. Its hero, Elec, is a small robot exploring a factory swallowed by darkness. Wherever Elec touches a floor, wall, or switch, electricity flows through the surface and brings dormant machinery to life. That single rule gives the surroundings an unusually direct relationship to the character: movement is not merely how you reach a solution, but part of the solution itself.

The stranger twist is that Elec can detach and throw his own head. A switch beyond a gap might suddenly be reachable, but the trick comes with a limit: if the robot fails to retrieve its head within ten seconds, it shuts down. The developer does not need a long inventory of tools to create a puzzle. A body that conducts, a head that travels, and a short deadline already allow many possibilities. In the official description, the challenge comes from discovering different uses for a small number of rules.

The pixel art follows the same philosophy. ElecHead favors spare, legible graphics instead of visual clutter. In a game about activating surfaces, clarity is part of how the player reasons: you need to understand which objects can be touched, which elements receive power, and where a thrown head might land. The restraint is more than a retro costume. It keeps attention on the relationship between a simple motion and its consequences.

The project has a longer history than its compact design suggests. Creator NamaTakahashi developed an early prototype for the 2016 Japan Game Awards Amateur Division, where it received an Excellence Award. A full commercial version followed on PC in October 2021. The developer also made a particularly welcoming decision: the game has no in-game text or tutorial, asking players to learn by interacting with its mechanisms rather than reading instructions.

The release announcement estimated two to three hours for a playthrough, with hidden spaces to discover beyond the main route. It is available through the creator's itch.io page, which also offers a demo, and on other storefronts. This feature is based on the developer's published material, not a claim to have played it. ElecHead looks worth investigating if you appreciate a game that starts with one odd idea and then asks, repeatedly, whether you have truly understood it.

title: Until Then
description: A Philippine-inspired high-school mystery where friendships, smartphone conversations, and ordinary errands collide with disappearing people and unreliable memories.
releaseStatus: Released · June 25, 2024 (PC/PS5); also available on Switch and Xbox
imageAlt: Original dreamy painterly editorial concept painting of students inside a rainy Philippine-inspired jeepney at violet dusk, with notebooks, window reflections, and glowing city lights; not gameplay
imageCredit: AI-generated editorial concept art — not official game artwork or gameplay
article: In Until Then, the frightening thing isn't initially a monster. It's the possibility that a friend, a conversation, or a remembered afternoon may not be as solid as it seemed. Polychroma Games sets its narrative adventure in a fictional Philippines still recovering from catastrophe. You follow Mark Borja, a high-school student whose immediate obligations are painfully ordinary: practice the piano, finish homework, keep friendships from collapsing. Then people begin to disappear, and his memories stop making dependable witnesses.

The structure is closer to a coming-of-age drama than an RPG. Conversations happen face to face, by text message, and through email; the in-game phone also holds social posts and webpages that can supply clues. Even idle online activity may have consequences, according to the official description. Between story scenes, there are deliberately mundane minigames: trying to insert a USB drive, competing for fishballs at a stall, and paying a jeepney fare. None is a world-saving superpower. The ordinary tasks make the place feel occupied.

Those specifics matter because the setting is not generic wallpaper. The creators describe spaces inspired by Metro Manila, Philippine landscapes, and their own school experiences. A commute, a school corridor, and the food outside a classroom become part of the story's texture. Players familiar with these routines might recognize home; others can observe a place presented through the particulars of living there, not a tourist brochure.

Pixel art does more than reference older consoles. Characters and props are hand-drawn, but they occupy a world with 3D depth, lighting, shadows, and reflections. That combination lets tiny gestures sit within spaces that feel larger than their sprite outlines. The visual approach isn't simply nostalgia. It is a way to make the places where ordinary relationships unfold matter just as much as the characters.

Until Then was released on June 25, 2024, and a demo is available on Steam. This description comes from the game's published materials, not a personal playthrough. For readers drawn to character-driven mystery, modern digital intimacy, and stories that let grief surface through everyday errands, it is worth investigating. What happens to friendship when even a shared memory cannot settle what happened yesterday?

title: Clear Skies
description: A small PICO-8 stargazing puzzle about finding real constellations with a telescope and guidebook, created in forty-eight hours for Ludum Dare 58.
releaseStatus: Released · October 5, 2025; browser play and Windows, macOS, Linux downloads
imageAlt: Original AI-generated painterly illustration of two stargazers beside a brass telescope on a lamplit wooden porch, with an open astronomy guide beneath a constellation-filled night sky; not gameplay
imageCredit: AI-generated editorial concept art — not official game artwork or gameplay
article: A star chart can turn an ordinary sky into a problem worth solving. In Clear Skies, a brief pixel-art game by Nash, you are far from city lights with a telescope given to you by your father and a guidebook called Your Guide to Clear Skies. The objective is to work out which stars you are seeing, and how they belong together. For a few minutes, a familiar sky becomes a field of small questions.

The controls are simple enough to remember: arrow keys move the telescope, X selects a star, and Z or C opens the guidebook or deselects. Read about a constellation, find its stars, and connect them. The creator describes the map as an eight-bit representation of a portion of the actual night sky. That is a more interesting promise than sheer graphical detail: a pattern can become recognizable even when each star is rendered as a tiny dot.

The guidebook supplies a little of the structure that beginning stargazers need. A constellation seems obvious after somebody traces its lines on a photograph. Scanning a stretch of sky for the correct starting points is a different skill. Clear Skies makes that search into a small puzzle instead of a lecture. It also offers a reason to go outside later: Nash says the constellations are ones players can try to locate in the real sky.

Nash made the game and all its assets in forty-eight hours for the Ludum Dare 58 Compo, using PICO-8 and Aseprite. According to the developer, it placed fourteenth for innovation and twenty-ninth overall in the jam. Those details suit its scale. There is no sprawling astronomy curriculum here, only a compact exercise with enough real-world correspondence to reward patient looking. Released on October 5, 2025, Clear Skies can be played in a browser, with name-your-own-price downloads available for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

This account is based on the creator's published information, not a completed playthrough. If you like quiet experiments, short educational games, or anything that makes a real hobby seem more approachable, Clear Skies deserves a look. You might come away knowing only a few additional patterns of stars. On the next genuinely clear night, that would be something you can use.
